posts.theme: Minnesota Somali business owners demand grants, eviction halt, ICE out
posts.quote: Somali Business Owners Demanded Direct Grants, No Evictions, And ICE Out.
posts.alt: Photo of Minnesota Sen. Omar Fateh in a gray jacket and black shirt, smiling in front of a Your Vote backdrop. Inset circle shows Gov. Tim Walz. Headline text: Somali Business Owners Demanded Direct Grants, No Evictions, And ICE Out.
posts.caption:
This was February. The demands are still on the group's website.

A Somali business group in Minneapolis, Neighbors United, started by members of the Somali community at Karmel Mall, told the state what it wanted after the ICE surge.

Direct grants. Not loans. Their written demand was for immigrant, Black, and brown businesses making under $200,000 a year, the ones they said were left out of Gov. Tim Walz's relief plan.

A halt on evictions, which they said Walz could do immediately by declaring a peacetime state of emergency.

And ICE out of Minnesota communities. They closed with a chant: "ICE out, families in. ICE out, small business in. ICE out, justice in."

Zahra Abdalla, who spoke at the news conference, said, "We have been suffering since the crisis of ICE."

Sen. Omar Fateh represents the district that includes Karmel Mall. I did not find him at that February news conference. In late January, he called for an eviction moratorium. "While they're scared to go out, their bills are piling up," he said. "This is why I'm calling for an eviction moratorium." In June, he wrote that the state's response was "too little too late," and that he wanted "more rent relief and monetary supports for small business and families impacted."

Walz wanted Washington to cover the bill. "The federal government needs to pay for what they broke here," he said. Minneapolis put the one-month hit at $203.1 million. His $10 million loan proposal for businesses making $250,000 to $4 million was never appropriated.

Vice President JD Vance's answer was blunt. "I would like reparations from them for allowing Somali fraudsters to steal billions of dollars from the American taxpayer that live in Minnesota. They've done nothing to cut down on that fraud."

They wanted cash, a freeze on evictions, and ICE gone. The governor wanted the feds to pay for an immigration crackdown. The vice president told them to look at the fraud first.
posts.first:
The facts: Neighbors United announced the demands at a Feb. 20, 2026, news conference at Karmel Mall in Minneapolis: direct grants, not loans, to immigrant, Black, and brown small businesses under $200,000; a halt to evictions through a peacetime emergency; and ICE out of Minnesota communities. Zahra Abdalla spoke. Sen. Omar Fateh, whose district includes Karmel Mall, is not documented at that event. In late January he called for an eviction moratorium. In June, he wrote that he wanted "more rent relief and monetary supports for small business and families impacted." Gov. Tim Walz said, "The federal government needs to pay for what they broke here." Minneapolis estimated at least $203.1 million in one-month impact. No 2026 session law appropriated Walz's $10 million loan package. Vice President JD Vance said he would like "reparations from them for allowing Somali fraudsters to steal billions of dollars from the American taxpayer that live in Minnesota."

Sources: Neighbors United, FOX 9, Minnesota Women's Press, Education Minnesota questionnaire, City of Minneapolis, RealClearPolitics / Fox News, Laws of Minnesota 2026.

posts.theme: Mamdani Rikers plan pays families to house relatives
posts.quote: Mamdani's Plan: Pay Families $500 A Month To House Relatives From Rikers.
posts.alt: Photo of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani in a dark suit and maroon tie, speaking at a microphone. Headline text: Mamdani's Plan: Pay Families $500 A Month To House Relatives From Rikers.
posts.caption:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plan to close Rikers Island has a line you should not miss.

He wants to expand a city program that pays family members to house relatives coming home from Rikers or prison. It would go from 50 families to 300. The city would put $3.55 million into it this fiscal year, then $7.1 million a year after that.

Families now get $500 a month for up to 12 months through the Osborne Association. City Hall has not said whether that number changes. The $7.1 million covers counseling and other services, not just the checks.

This is in the official plan, released Nov. 20. It is a plan to pay families, not random neighbors.

Council Minority Leader David Carr called it "another reckless use of taxpayer money on a social experiment that could go horribly wrong." Councilman Phil Wong, a Democrat, said, "Only in New York City do we come up with a program that pays families to take in their own relatives coming out of jail."
posts.first:
The facts: The Close Rikers Strategic Plan, released Nov. 20, 2026, says: "Invest $3.55M in FY27 and $7.1M annually thereafter to expand the Kinship Reentry Housing Program from supporting 50 to 300 families." The plan says it "provides a stable home for people returning to community from Rikers or prison." The official population target is about 6,600 down to no more than 4,100 by the end of 2032.

Sources: Close Rikers Strategic Plan, NYC Mayor's Office, New York Post, Osborne Association.
